notes.meaning: Once the riot in Ephesus settled down, Paul gathered the believers together to encourage them and say goodbye. He had spent years planting and strengthening the church there, but now it was time to move on to Macedonia. Even after facing mob violence, his main concern was to show love to the disciples and leave them in good spirits.

Paul traveled across the northern region of Macedonia, encouraging the believers in cities like Philippi and Thessalonica. After spending time building up those young congregations, he headed south into Greece. He stayed mainly in the city of Corinth to continue his pastoral work.

Paul stayed in Greece for three months, during which he likely wrote his letter to the Romans. As he prepared to sail straight for Syria, he discovered that hostile Jewish opponents had plotted an ambush against him on the ship. To protect his life and avoid the trap, he changed his plans and decided to journey back overland through Macedonia.

A group of trusted Christian companions traveled with Paul, representing different churches from Macedonia and Asia Minor. Several of these men helped carry the money collected by Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Traveling together let Paul mentor these future leaders and show complete openness in handling the collection.

The other traveling companions sailed ahead to wait in Troas, while Paul and Luke stayed behind in Philippi through the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Luke uses the word 'we' again here, showing he had rejoined Paul on the road. Once the festival ended, they sailed across the Aegean Sea in five days and spent a full week together in Troas.

The believers gathered on the first day of the week, which is Sunday, to celebrate the Lord's Supper and hear God's word. Because Sunday was an ordinary workday in the Roman empire, they met in the evening. Since Paul planned to leave the next morning, he kept teaching the group until midnight.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the phrase 'first day of the week' according to Jewish evening-to-evening time reckoning, which would place this meeting on Saturday night rather than Sunday night.

notes.meaning: The upstairs room where they met was lit by many oil lamps. These lamps provided the light needed to read scripture, share communion, and see everyone clearly. However, burning so many lamps in a crowded room also made the air hot and smoky.

A young man named Eutychus sat in an open window recess, probably looking for fresh air away from the heat. As Paul's sermon went on late into the night, Eutychus was overcome by deep sleep and fell out of the window. He dropped three stories to the ground below and was found completely dead.

Paul rushed downstairs and threw himself upon the young man, embracing him just as the old prophets Elijah and Elisha had done. He told the frightened crowd to stop panicking because the boy was alive again. God had worked through Paul to bring life back into the dead youth.

Paul went back upstairs, broke the bread for communion, and ate food for bodily refreshment. Greatly encouraged, he spent the rest of the night talking and teaching the church until sunrise. When morning arrived, he set out on his journey without taking any sleep.

The believers were filled with deep relief and comfort when they were able to take the young man home alive. God had turned a heartbreaking accident into a powerful sign of his life-giving power. The miracle confirmed the truth of the gospel message Paul had been preaching.

Luke and the rest of the team boarded a ship to sail south around the coastline toward Assos. Paul chose to travel the shorter land route on foot to meet them there later. Walking by foot gave Paul valuable quiet time for prayer and reflection, or extra moments to visit local friends.

Paul met up with his companions at Assos as planned and came aboard their ship, which then set sail for Mitylene on the island of Lesbos. Over the next few days, they navigated past the islands of Chios and Samos before finally docking at Miletus on the mainland coast.

Paul decided to sail right past Ephesus so he would not be delayed in the province of Asia. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem in time for the Feast of Pentecost, which was one of the great Jewish pilgrimage festivals. He wanted to use the large crowds gathered there as an opportunity to share Christ.

While docked at Miletus, Paul sent word about thirty miles north to Ephesus, calling for the elders of the church to meet him. These elders were the local pastors and overseers charged with caring for the congregation. Meeting them in Miletus gave Paul a final chance to guide these leaders without being detained at Ephesus.

differ.view: Some Anglicans hold that while local elders and overseers were the same in the early church, apostles like Paul functioned as bishops with authority over those pastors.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that 'elder' refers to the ordained priesthood, while 'overseer' describes their pastoral duty of supervision over the flock.

notes.meaning: When the elders arrived, Paul began by reminding them of his daily life and conduct from the moment he first arrived in Asia. He had lived openly among them at all times, with nothing hidden or fake. His faithful way of living gave weight and honesty to the message he had preached.

Paul served the Lord with genuine humility, never seeking worldly glory, wealth, or personal power. His ministry had included many tears and severe trials caused by hostile plots against him. Yet through every threat and hardship, he kept serving his Master faithfully.

Paul never held back any truth that would help his hearers grow in faith, even when that truth was difficult to hear. He taught both in public gatherings and in private homes, meeting with believers face-to-face. He showed deep concern for the entire church community as well as individual families.

Paul preached the exact same life-giving message to both Jews and Gentiles without playing favorites. He urged all people to repent—which means turning away from sin and toward God—and to place their full trust in the Lord Jesus Christ. These two responses form the very heart of the gospel.

Paul felt strongly compelled by the Holy Spirit to journey on to Jerusalem. He did not know what specific events or dangers would meet him once he arrived. Even with the future hidden from his eyes, he obeyed God's inner call with a willing heart.

The only certainty Paul had was that prison chains and hardships were waiting for him. In town after town, Christian prophets warned him through the Holy Spirit about the trials ahead. Knowing the danger in advance did not frighten him, but helped prepare his soul to suffer for Christ.

Paul counted his physical life of no supreme value compared to finishing the race God had set before him. His greatest aim was to complete the assignment given him by the Lord Jesus, which was to testify to God's free grace. Faithfully serving Christ mattered far more to him than staying safe or comfortable.

Paul told the elders plainly that none of them would ever see his face again in this life. He had spent years preaching the kingdom of God among them, but that chapter of his work had now ended. This solemn parting statement was meant to make them take his final instructions to heart.

Because Paul had held nothing back, he declared himself free from guilt if anyone should perish. He was thinking of God's command to the prophet Ezekiel, where a watchman must warn the people or bear the blame for their death. Paul had faithfully sounded the alarm, so their spiritual choices rested entirely on them.

Paul was completely innocent of their spiritual ruin because he had declared God's entire plan of salvation to them. He never watered down hard teachings to please people or stay popular. He laid out the whole message of what God has done to rescue sinners.

Paul charged the elders to watch carefully over their own spiritual lives first and then care for the whole flock. The Holy Spirit had made them overseers and shepherds of God's church. This people is infinitely precious because God purchased it through the blood of his own Son on the cross.

differ.view: Reformed Christians point to this verse to show that Christ's blood was shed to secure and redeem a definite, chosen flock.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient manuscripts vary between 'church of God' and 'church of the Lord', and prefer translating the final phrase as 'the blood of his own Son.'

notes.meaning: Paul warned that after he departed, dangerous false teachers would attack the church like fierce wolves. Instead of caring for the believers, these deceivers would harm and exploit the flock. Leaders must always stay on guard against destructive outside influences trying to slip into the church.

The danger would also arise from inside the church itself, even among respected leaders. Men would twist God's truth to build a personal following and pull disciples away from Christ. Paul warned that pride and division inside the family of faith are often the church's greatest threats.

Paul urged the elders to stay constantly awake and alert. He reminded them that for three full years he had never stopped warning each one of them day and night with tears. His tireless love and watchful care provided the exact pattern they were called to follow.

Knowing he could no longer protect them in person, Paul entrusted the elders into God's safe keeping and to the message of his grace. God's word has the power to build believers up in strength and secure their final heavenly inheritance. Only God's grace can keep his people firm against every enemy.

Paul pointed out that he had never used his ministry to get rich. He had never craved anyone's silver, gold, or fine garments. His conscience was clear because his motives for preaching had always been completely unselfish.

The elders knew firsthand that Paul worked with his own hands as a tentmaker to provide for his basic needs. He earned his own food and clothes so he would not be a financial burden to the church, and he even helped provide for his traveling companions. Working hard showed that he loved the people, not their money.

By his hard work, Paul showed church leaders how to help the poor, sick, and vulnerable. He reminded them of a saying of Jesus not found in the four Gospels: giving brings greater joy and blessing than receiving. Faithful leaders use their strength to serve and lift up others rather than taking from them.

When Paul finished his farewell speech, he knelt down on the ground with all the elders and prayed. Kneeling was a natural posture of deep humility, reverence, and earnest petition before God. Together, they poured out their hearts and committed each other into the Lord's hands.

Overcome with sorrow and love, all the elders wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him. True Christian faith does not stamp out deep feelings, but makes love tender and strong. They loved Paul deeply as their spiritual father and faithful shepherd.

What caused the elders the deepest grief was Paul's statement that they would never see his face again on earth. With heavy hearts, they walked beside him all the way to the ship to see him off. Their tearful farewell showed how deeply Christian hearts are joined together in shared gospel ministry.
